statements.quote: As a doctor who took the long road coming to medical school, I realize now that some of my pre-medicine experiences will prove helpful in my career as a child psychiatrist.
statements.context: Republished 2014 residency personal statement (post dated 2023-02-12 reprints it with commentary). The author, then an applicant, predicts that his pre-medicine work (arts-education grants and school-district research with Litchfield Performing Arts) will prove useful in his career as a child psychiatrist.
statements.note: Personal career claim from a 2014 document republished in 2023; low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Child Psychiatry training will provide me with the expertise to hone my pre-existing skills in humor, quick, “improvisational” thinking, systems-based care, and evidence-based practice in a way that can promote resiliency in the face of mental illness and demystify the road to recovery for patients and their caregivers.
statements.context: Closing paragraph of the 2014 personal statement: child psychiatry training will give the author the expertise to promote resiliency and demystify recovery for patients and caregivers. The 2023 commentary adds: 'I can stand behind this last paragraph to this day.'
statements.note: 2014 forecast about the author's own training, endorsed in the 2023 commentary; the training horizon elapsed before the post date, so forward_looking is false.

statements.quote: Clearly, the path forward toward the best care for severely ill patients with mood and psychotic disorders isn't always easiest or most obvious treatment, and it will take well-informed child psychiatrists to advocate for these options.
statements.context: In the 2014 personal statement, after a survey at Zucker Hillside Hospital in which over 30% of caregivers saw benefits in long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics for first-episode youth, the author claims that wider use of these options will require well-informed child psychiatrists to advocate for them.
statements.note: Borderline: truism-like claim about a necessary condition for LAI adoption in youth; from the 2014 text republished in 2023.

statements.quote: It doesn’t even matter if a journalist figures it out—because they won’t even care!
statements.context: The author describes the Pew Charitable Trusts' covert campaign-finance-reform playbook (secretly funded experts, groups, reports and ads) and proposes reusing it for healthcare lobbying. He predicts that exposure by a journalist would not matter because nobody would care.
statements.note: Borderline: generic prediction about journalist and public reaction to an astroturf healthcare campaign; no date or specific event. Author says 'I’m not actually criticizing the above'.

statements.quote: Now, can we fix Healthcare? The Pew Charitable Trusts got campaign finance reform passed with a budget of millions, not billions! We just need to take our propaganda seriously and target it at the decision makers who matter.
statements.context: Closing argument of the post: the author asks whether healthcare can be fixed and implies yes, since Pew got campaign finance reform passed for millions of dollars; the implicit conditional is that a serious, targeted propaganda effort aimed at decision makers would achieve healthcare reform.
statements.note: Implicit conditional call framed as a question plus 'we just need to'; borderline normative.

statements.quote: Authorization will be issued for 12 months, Expiring on 2/13/2024. Subsequent Romantic Dates and/or Gestures will require matchmaker-to-matchmaker review.
statements.context: Satirical fake UnitedHealthcare prior-authorization denial for a Valentine's dinner with the author's wife Carlene MacMillan. The parody letter states that authorization will run 12 months, expiring 2/13/2024, and that later dates will need 'matchmaker-to-matchmaker review'.
statements.note: Satire; logged for completeness only. Other future-tense lines in the parody ('will be approved based on ALL of the following criteria') are of the same kind and were not logged.

statements.quote: I have bipolar disorder. I've written about it before . I will write about it again.
statements.context: Early in the lithium guide, the author discloses his own bipolar disorder and commits to writing about it again in the newsletter.
statements.note: Own newsletter content plan; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Lithium data says: treating symptoms is the wrong approach, it always has been, and it always will be, because people's lives aren't about symptoms.
statements.context: In the section arguing that lithium cuts suicide deaths without treating bipolar depression well, the author claims that symptom-focused psychiatry is the wrong approach and always will be.
statements.note: Borderline: philosophical stance phrased as a permanent future claim; low resolvability.

statements.quote: Or whatever the limit is on the size of the pill. It will not be a money maker, but it will be important.
statements.context: The author proposes a hypothetical lithium product, 'Dr. M’s Lith-o-sure', an Eskalith CR-like formulation in larger strengths (600mg to 1400mg), addressed to Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drugs team. He predicts such a product would not be profitable but would be important.
statements.note: Conditional on a hypothetical product no company has announced; a wish plus a forecast about its commercial value.

statements.quote: I think the better future of healthcare includes “adherence augmentation” with technologies like iRxReminder (a company at which I’m now Chief Medical Officer).
statements.context: Disclosure section headed 'The Most Commercially Biased Opinion': the author predicts that the better future of healthcare includes adherence-augmentation technologies such as iRxReminder, where he is Chief Medical Officer.
statements.note: Author's own company; coder marks CONTROL. The author himself labels it commercially biased.

statements.quote: It was easier to evaluate this when all psychiatry was in person, but when it comes to tele-health, we're gonna need to do a better job of collecting this data.
statements.context: Tremor side-effect section: lithium tremor is dose-dependent and was easier to assess in person; the author says telehealth psychiatry will need better collection of tremor data.
statements.note: Normative with a weak predictive reading about telehealth practice; logged for recall.

statements.quote: These are reasonable options if this side effect presents itself. Expect to fight for prior authorization.
statements.context: Erectile dysfunction side-effect section: Viagra and Stendra are options for lithium-related sexual dysfunction; the author tells prescribers to expect prior-authorization fights from payers for these drugs.
statements.note: Generic expectation about payer prior-authorization behavior; imperative form with a predictive reading.

statements.quote: The Frontier Psychiatrists is a newsletter for our life and complex times. And it’s probably going to pay off if you subscribe. But the PPV for that isn’t perfect
statements.context: Sign-off after the screening and Bayesian explainer: the author says subscribing to The Frontier Psychiatrists will probably pay off, then undercuts it with a positive-predictive-value joke.
statements.note: Newsletter self-promotion in joke form; coder may mark CONTROL; very low forecast value.
